#9101. Julia Stoschek Foundation to reopen Düsseldorf headquarters in 2027

The title of Sarah Lucas’s Selfish in Bed II (2000) has inspired the foundation’s first exhibition at the reopened Düsseldorf location Courtesy of Julia Stoschek Foundation; © The artist

A month after closing its Berlin exhibition space, the Julia Stoschek Foundation, a nonprofit arts organisation set up by the German collector and businesswoman Julia Stoschek, announced it will reopen its Düsseldorf headquarters in April 2027.

The Düsseldorf space closed for renovation in 2025. The inaugural exhibition in the newly revamped space, called Selfish in Bed, is curated by Krist Gruijthuijsen, formerly the director of the KW Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin will feature works by 43 artists from the foundation’s collection. The foundation’s more than 1,000-piece collection is focused primarily on time-based art—including video, film, moving-image installations, multimedia work, performance, sound work and virtual reality work.

“Seeing the collection continue to grow and welcoming new audiences two decades on brings me enormous joy,” Stoschek said in a statement. “And I can think of no better home for it than Düsseldorf, a city where art has been part of everyday life for generations.”

Stoschek’s Berlin space operated for ten years from June 2016 to October 2026. It hosted 22 exhibitions and drew 500,000 visitors. In April, the foundation said the closure was the result of a “strategic realignment” and that it would “now focus on international projects in order to make the collection accessible to a global audience.”

The Düsseldorf reopening marks the foundation’s 20th anniversary.

Selfish in Bed (10 April 2027-19 December 2027) takes its name from a 2000 self-portrait by Sarah Lucas. Other artists who will feature in the exhibition include Wolfgang Tillmans, Bill Viola, Simon Fujiwara, Rosemarie Trockel and Tracey Emin.

#9093. Venice exhibition tells the story of the man who brought together contemporary artists and Murano’s master glassblowers

Jean Cocteau with the glass master Ermanno Nason in Murano, around 1957 © Archivio Fucina degli Angeli, Venezia, by SIAE 2026

In 1952, Egidio Costantini, an entrepreneur based in Venice, had a brainwave: to take the designs of contemporary artists and, with the collaboration of master glassblowers on the island of Murano, to make artistic sculptures in glass. This was a different approach from that adopted by traditional furnaces like Venini in their decorative glassware, which, although it increasingly involved international designers, was often produced in large, commercially dictated series.

Three years later, Costantini established the Fucina degli Angeli gallery to exhibit the results of his experiment. From then until the 1970s, when other glassmaking companies began to compete, Costantini played a pioneering role in the evolution of glass in Venice, acting as interpreter for more than 100 international artists to Murano’s master glassblowers.

An exhibition opening at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice this month, curated by the art historian Cristina Beltrami, will tell the Fucina’s story from the 1950s to the 1980s. It will also examine the little-documented but vital role played behind the scenes by Peggy Guggenheim herself, whose purchase of many items helped sustain the gallery financially and whose connections enabled Costantini to exhibit his glass across Europe and even in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. (As it happens, the collector is also the focus of an exhibition opening this month at the Royal Academy of Arts in London, about her Mayfair gallery of the late 1930s—Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector, 21 November-14 March 2027.)

More than 100 works, including glass, painting and sculpture, will be on display in Venice, as well as material from the Fucina’s archives, which have never before been studied in depth. These will be exhibited in 11 rooms organised by artist and theme, and will include glass translations of works by many luminaries of the period, from Max Ernst and Oskar Kokoschka to Lucio Fontana and Paul Jenkins.

Peggy Guggenheim among her glass artworks and guests at Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, Venice, in 1964 © Getty Images, by SIAE 2026

Born in Brindisi in the south of Italy in 1912, Costantini established himself permanently in Venice, where he had been raised and educated, at the beginning of the 1950s. There he became a commercial agent for several of Murano’s glassworks. It was the time of Italy’s post-war economic boom and the city was teeming with creative energy. Costantini seems to have found no difficulty in assembling a group of Venetian artists to form the Study Centre for Painters in the Art of Glass, a collective that exhibited its work at the furnace of Ferro & Lazzarini in 1953.

The next step was to involve international artists of even greater stature. Acting on his own initiative, Costantini had glass versions made of some ceramic sculptures by Pablo Picasso and then travelled to Picasso’s house in Vallauris, near Cannes, to show him the results. In return, Picasso gave Costantini a copy of the book Faunes et Nymphes de Pablo Picasso (1952). This survives in the archives with markings on the images of ceramic figures that were later reinterpreted as glass sculptures at the Fucina. But who made the markings remains a mystery.

The name “Fucina degli Angeli” (smithy of the angels) was proposed by the French writer and artist Jean Cocteau, a long-term friend and collaborator, apparently in reference to Costantini’s large family. The Austrian Expressionist artist Kokoschka contributed an emblematic sketch of two angels holding up an anvil, which he dedicated to the gallery and its founder, “who first succeeded in making me fascinated with the glass of Murano”.

Max Ernst’s King (Re) and Queen (Regina), both from 1964 © Max Ernst, by SIAE 2026

Cocteau enjoyed designing extravagant mythological heads for the Fucina, as well as visiting the furnaces and discussing his ideas with the maestri. Both he and Jean Arp, the German sculptor and painter whose work also features in the exhibition, were “seduced by the colour” of glass and its richness, Beltrami says.

The results, though, may not have pleased everyone. The Swiss artist Walter Bodmer allowed his sketch Asymmetric Cat (1955) to be transformed into an oversimplified glass vessel. But after this, for reasons unknown, he never participated again.

The exhibition looks set to offer a fascinating insight into a very personal approach to collaborations between artist and craftsman, as well as an evocative record of an under-appreciated chapter in Venetian history.

• Fucina degli Angeli: Peggy Guggenheim and 20th-Century Artistic Glass, Peggy Guggenheim Collection, Venice, 14 November-29 March 2027

#9091. Adobe’s Quiet Lightroom Classic Updates Are a Big Deal for Photographers

Adobe’s Quiet Lightroom Classic Updates Are a Big Deal for Photographers

Adobe’s MAX press kit focused on just a few updates to Lightroom and gave Lightroom Classic no specific attention, but that doesn’t mean that the popular RAW editing and organization app hasn’t received big changes. Lightroom Classic 16.0 is here, and it includes a ton of meaningful improvements.

Lightroom Classic 16.0 includes some of the changes that Adobe did talk about in its MAX press release, including the new Glow and Blemish Removal tools, but it includes so much more.

The changes start as soon as a photographer goes to add new photos to their Lightroom catalog. Users can now filter their photos before they import them, with Lightroom Classic 16.0 recognizing and preserving in-camera ratings, color labels, protected status, and file types. These filters also carry over to Lightroom Classic’s relatively new Assisted Culling workflow, promising even faster results and less bloated catalogs.

Speaking of bloated catalogs, Lightroom Classic 16 also lets users clean up history states on photos they’ve edited while preserving the final appearance. Adobe says that by clearing history states for multiple photos, folders, or even entire collections, users can significantly reduce the file size of their catalogs. It’s also possible to schedule automatic cleanup of history states, ensuring that catalogs stay lean without deleting data that might be useful during a specific project.

Lightroom Classic now includes a vectorscope, which photographers can use to analyze the colors and skin tones in their photos. Although vectorscopes might already be familiar to DaVinci Resolve users, they can be a little intimidating at first. Essentially, neutral colors—such as black, gray, and white—live at the center of the scope. The farther a color is from the center, the more saturated it is, while the direction from the center reflects the color’s hue.

Adobe has a detailed breakdown of how to use Lightroom’s new vectorscope on its support website, but the main takeaway is that the vectorscope will make it easier for some users to analyze and edit colors, including across multiple color spaces.

The newly updated Lightroom Classic also offers new ways for photographers to edit the colors in their images. It’s now easier to add color tints only to masked areas in any image using the existing Color Grading tools. Editors can tweak color grades for shadows, midtones, and highlights within a selected masked area of the frame.

Lightroom Classic 16 also includes new ways to manage and customize the app’s Masking panel. Photographers can rearrange controls and add their most-used sliders to a Favorites section for quicker access.

While existing subject detection and masking tools have long made it easy for photographers to perform specific localized edits inside Lightroom Classic, Adobe is adding an AI-powered depth masking tool to let users select and edit the foreground, middle ground, or background in their photos.

This can be performed on any photo, and users can customize and refine the depth mask manually. However, in some cases, photo files already include depth information, which Lightroom Classic recognizes and uses to create its depth mask.

Lightroom Classic can now also show users the focus point data recorded in RAW files by the camera, at least with select cameras. As of now, RAW photos from Canon, Nikon, and Sony cameras that record autofocus data work with focus point viewing.

In the Transform panel, there’s a new Projection slider that users can adjust to fix distorted faces and objects near the edge of the frame, especially when using a wide-angle lens.

As always, the Lightroom Classic update brings new camera and lens support as well. In this case, it’s a short list of new cameras, with just the Apple iPhone Duo’s Ultrawide and Wide cameras getting new support in Adobe Camera Raw 19.0 inside Lightroom Classic 16.0.

On the lens side of things, Apple’s new iPhone Duo cameras are supported, of course, but so are lenses from Laowa, Sigma, Sony, and Tamron. Of note are Sony’s new FE 8-14mm f/3.5 Fisheye G, FE 400mm f/4.5 GM, and FE 600mm f/6.3 GM lenses. Sigma’s new 50-120mm f/2.8 DC OS and Tamron’s new 17-70mm f/2.8 RF lenses are supported, too.

As mentioned in PetaPixel‘s other MAX coverage today, the Glow tool added earlier this year to Adobe Camera Raw has arrived in Lightroom, letting users add a soft glow around highlight areas in their photos with customizable controls. Blemish Removal, introduced in Lightroom for mobile, is now in Lightroom on desktop as well, including Lightroom Classic.

Image creditsAdobe with additional illustrative example photos by Jeremy Gray.

#9089. All of Adobe Camera RAW’s Awesome Updates Adobe Didn’t Mention

All of Adobe Camera RAW’s Awesome Updates Adobe Didn’t Mention

The good news keeps coming for photographers using Adobe’s software. Alongside big Lightroom Classic updates, Adobe Camera Raw (ACR) has been updated today to version 19.0, ushering in a wide range of tweaks, some of which are major.

Adobe Camera Raw is an extremely important part of Adobe Photoshop for photography workflows, especially for photographers who capture RAW photos. The underlying RAW processing and editing technologies found in ACR overlap heavily with Lightroom, although sometimes a feature arrives first in ACR, like Glow, which debuted in Adobe Camera Raw a few months ago before coming to Lightroom today. Another example is Reflection Removal, which arrived first in Adobe Camera Raw before eventually making it into other Adobe photography apps.

Speaking of Glow, it has been upgraded today. There are new Motion and Streak styles. Users can fine-tune the length, direction, color, and softness of the new Glow variants.

In terms of all-new Adobe Camera Raw features, it’s a bulky list. Virtual Copies, a longtime feature for creating multiple versions of photos inside Lightroom without duplicating original files, are now in Adobe Camera Raw. Each version’s edits can be preserved between sessions as well.

Generative Remove selections can now be applied to all selected photos inside a batch within ACR. So, for example, if a photographer has a group of photos that all have the same distracting element, such as a telephone pole, it’s possible to select the element in one photo, remove it, and then apply the same process to the entire group without needing to manually mask and remove it from each shot.

It’s also now possible to organize photos inside an ACR session. Related or similar photos can be grouped into stacks manually or automatically using capture metadata. It’s worth noting that Auto-Stack by Capture Metadata is currently only supported for recent Canon and Nikon cameras that support the DNG file format. However, all photographers can still group photos into stacks manually.

For those who use Adobe Camera Raw to process many photos at once, navigating through a crowded filmstrip or Grid view can be tedious. ACR 19.0 lets users temporarily hide photos or show only selected shots during a session, which significantly cleans up the workspace.

Finally, Adobe Camera Raw 19.0 introduces new camera and lens support. The list of newly supported cameras is very short, including just the two cameras on the new Apple iPhone Duo. However, new lens support has arrived for Sony’s new FE 8-14mm f/3.5 Fisheye G lens, FE 400mm f/4.5 GM and FE 600mm f/6.3 GM telephoto primes, and new zooms from Sigma and Tamron. There’s also support for Laowa’s 50mm f/2.8 2x Ultra-Macro APO lens across many mounts.

#9086. Ring’s AI-Powered Drone Automatically Patrols Inside Your Home

Ring’s AI-Powered Drone Automatically Patrols Inside Your Home

Home security can now fly. Amazon-owned Ring has announced the Ring Drone Cam, a $250 indoor flying security camera designed to automatically patrol a home’s interior.

The AI-powered Ring Drone Cam works alongside existing Ring products, including static cameras and sensors. When an alarm sounds or motion is detected, the drone automatically deploys to investigate.

Homeowners can also launch the drone on command or program custom flight routines on a scheduled basis. Due to its compact, lightweight design, flight times are limited to eight minutes per charge. Users can monitor a live 360-degree feed on their smartphones while the drone is airborne, and built-in LED spotlights allow it to operate effectively in total darkness.

Although designed to operate autonomously, initial setup requires some manual effort: users must carry the drone throughout their home to help it build an internal spatial map. Additionally, Ring notes that navigation works best in environments with distinct visual details; reflective surfaces, featureless walls, and frameless glass may pose operational challenges.

Detailed camera specifications remain sparse, but Ring confirms the drone features a 2K (1920×1920) square image sensor paired with a 148-degree field of view.

After completing a patrol, the drone automatically returns to its base station, fully recharging in roughly an hour. Ring emphasizes that all video and audio recording automatically stops whenever the drone is docked.

With a subscription, users can store, share, and review recorded footage—including motion events and Live View feeds—for up to 180 days. Users can also search through archival footage using plain-text queries.

Designed exclusively for indoor use, the premise behind the Ring Drone Cam is simple: a single autonomous drone can monitor the same space as multiple stationary security cameras.

Ring founder Jamie Siminoff told The Verge during a launch event that the company has spent a decade developing the drone off and on, only recently achieving its design and performance goals after returning to the drawing board a year ago.

Although Amazon’s listing notes the device has not yet received FCC authorization, Siminoff states that the U.S.-assembled drone complies with all regulatory standards.

The Ring Drone Cam is scheduled to ship in January 2027 for $249.99.

#9084. VSCO Updates Its Policy to Explicitly State It Won’t Train AI on Your Photos

VSCO Updates Its Policy to Explicitly State It Won’t Train AI on Your Photos

In May, VSCO came under scrutiny for wording in its Terms of Use that seemed to give the company permission to use certain user content to develop, train, and improve generative AI or machine learning models. It has now taken the extra step to clarify that it doesn’t do that, and won’t.

It was noticed that VSCO’s Terms of Use stated that users granted VSCO the right to use the “name, image, voice, or likeness of any individual in your Content, in whole or in part, and in any form, media, or technology, whether now known or developed in the future.” It also included “the right” for VSCO to “use certain Content for Creator Promotion and to develop, train, and improve AI or machine learning models as further described in our Creator Content Standards.”

This, of course, set off some alarm bells and the company quickly said it wouldn’t be training AI models on users’ content. For some, this might not have been enough, however, and VSCO seems to have taken note of that.

“You deserve a straight answer about what happens to the work you put on VSCO,” Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, writes in a letter sent to VSCO users today. “Sharing your work shouldn’t mean wondering whether it will be used to train a system designed to generate content (photos or video) without you.”

As a result, the company has today updated its Creator Content Standards to more explicitly state this stance.

“We don’t use your content to train generative AI models. Not your public work. Not your private work. Not because you have a paid membership. The same protection applies whether you pay us or not,” Wittman continues.

“We’re updating our Creator Content Standards to make that explicit.”

The updated Content Creator Standards page now says the following:

If you are a paid member with an active VSCO membership or a non-paying Creator on VSCO, your Public or Private Creator Content will not be utilized to develop, train, or improve AI or machine learning models for Generative AI Use.

“For the past 15 years we have championed photographers. That means building a business around helping you make your work and earn from it. It doesn’t mean treating the photographs you entrust to us as raw material for models that generate images, video or other media. It’s a good moment to also be precise about what we mean by generative AI because AI isn’t one thing, and calling out the distinction matters,” he writes.

“We use machine learning technology and non-generative AI across the VSCO platform with the goal of helping photographers, whether that’s to find work, search for people to connect with, edit images and get more out of our products. We have heard from the photography community this is where AI is useful. That’s very different from using your photographs to train models that generate new content. Our updated standards make that boundary explicit.”

VSCO says that it isn’t just holding itself to these standards, but anyone the company works with, too.

“We’re holding our providers to that distinction, too. Outside AI providers who have been powering VSCO features have already agreed not to use content submitted through our services to train generative AI models. Language in our previous Creator Content Standards was too broad to make these distinctions and intentions clear. That left room for confusion about where we stood. You shouldn’t have to decipher a policy to find out what is happening with your work on a platform you use,” Wittman says.

“Your work isn’t just a file on our platform. It represents the time you spent learning, the places you went to, the people who trusted you and the choices only you could make. That perspective and what you choose to do with it is yours.”

VSCO’s updated Creator Content Standards can be read on the company’s website.

#9081. Art Basel offers compensation to dealers after early closure of Paris fair

Art Basel Paris 2026 was shut early due to protests in the French capital

Art Basel will compensate dealers for the early closure of its Paris fair, held from 20-23 October in the Grand Palais, the fair company announced today (11th November), on a French national holiday.

The fair was forced to shut down its Parisian outing two days early because of violent rioting in the French capital. Since then, dealers have been demanding compensation for their lost sales and stand fees. Indeed, soon after the closure the French Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA) sent a strongly worded letter to the fair director, Karim Crippa. It accused the firm of not consulting with dealers—the CPGA represents 57 of the fair’s 211 exhibitors—and of showing “disrespect, even contempt” for them.

The closure hit the smaller dealers particularly hard, since the biggest galleries tended to make sales on the opening days, whereas the smaller dealers, mainly sited on the upper floor of the Grand Palais, depended on the two weekend days for business. The letter said it expected “concrete proposals” for this compensation.

Crippa has responded to the letter with an offer of a reduction across the board of 20% of stand fees to all participants. He said: “We believe this approach offers a fair and considered way forward, reflecting our appreciation of the partnership we share and our commitment to strengthening it further.”

Philippe Charpentier of Mor Charpentier gallery, who is the president of the CPGA, tells The Art Newspaper that the compensation rate is what the committee expected.

Nonetheless, if one calculates in percentages, the fair was open for three-and-a-half days—its ultra-VIP Avant-Première timeslot began at 3pm on Tuesday 20 October, and the fair closed on Friday—instead of the projected five-and-a-half. The fair was therefore shortened by about 36%.

Speaking about the decision to close the fair early, Noah Horowitz, the chief executive of Art Basel, tells The Art Newspaper: “We stand by the decision to close. We feel it was in the right interest of all the parties involved. It was a very difficult decision, but we stand by it.”

Asked about the decision to close for the two days—when unrest was only expected on the Saturday—he says: “Given the uncertainty surrounding the impact and the duration of the planned demonstrations and access to the Grand Palais, we simply couldn't be confident that conditions would allow us to reopen safely on Sunday. An event of this size and scale is incredibly complex, and some exhibitors had also expressed serious concerns about leaving artworks unattended in the Grand Palais on the weekend. We concluded that closing the fair early was in the best interests of the art, the staff and ultimately the visitors.”

Horowitz is not prepared to comment on other aspects of the closure—for example, questions of insurance or the firm’s relationship with the Grand Palais, for which MCH paid €10.6m to rent the space for seven years in 2022. Horowitz says that MCH, the parent company of the Basel group of art fairs, is "fully committed to delivering the 2027 edition of the fair".

#9080. Forma Is a Wearable Viewfinder Built for Finding Photo Compositions

Forma Is a Wearable Viewfinder Built for Finding Photo Compositions

Canadian photographer and inventor Peter Modzelewski has launched Forma on Kickstarter via his independent photo gear studio, Oramod. It is a pocket-sized optical viewfinder designed for a wide range of film and digital cameras.

Forma utilizes interchangeable, laser-cut cards tailored to specific formats and focal lengths, ranging from 35mm film cameras to large-format and specialized panoramic systems.

Photographers can simply hold Forma up to their eye to accurately preview a composition without setting up their camera—a process that can be quite an ordeal with certain medium- and large-format systems. It can also be used when scouting locations to help photographers determine where to position their gear in advance.

Forma can also be used on cameras without viewfinders, spanning specialized analog cameras to modern digital compacts like the Ricoh GR series.

As Modzelewski explains, Forma is constructed from a 3D-printed, carbon-fiber-infused composite material, offering a rugged yet lightweight design weighing just 30 grams (just over an ounce). It is built on the binocular fusion principle used in Voigtländer’s Kontur viewfinder from 1951. However, unlike the Kontur, Forma is highly configurable thanks to its interchangeable framing cards.

Forma features built-in illumination for low-light conditions, gels that color-tint the framelines for visibility in various environments, and a quick-release mounting system that allows photographers to switch between wearing it around the neck and attaching it to a camera in seconds.

“Worn around the neck, Forma helps photographers train their eye to recognize what their lenses will see, explore compositions before setting up a camera, and compare focal lengths by easily swapping cards,” Modzelewski says.

“Mounted on-camera, Forma provides a framing reference while allowing photographers to anticipate moments unfolding beyond the boundaries of a conventional viewfinder.”

Modzelewski sent pre-production units to photographers worldwide for real-world testing, including Japanese photographer Kazutoshi Yoshimura and British landscape photographer Lee Pengelly.

“I was amazed at how clearly I could see the field of view corresponding to the focal length of my lens,” Yoshimura says.

“It will be an essential part of my kit from now on,” adds Pengelly.

Utah-based large-format photographer James Holland touted Forma’s accuracy, noting that he didn’t have to move his tripod “an inch” when framing with it.

Forma is available to back on Kickstarter now, starting at $55 CAD (approximately $39 USD) for early birds. The campaign reached its funding goal quickly on launch day and has nearly 60 backers at the time of writing. Forma is expected to begin shipping to backers next month.

#9077. Inside OM Digital Solutions’ Okaya Manufacturing Site

Inside OM Digital Solutions’ Okaya Manufacturing Site

I know how to take pictures, but ask me how the lens on my camera is made and I have a lot less to say. A visit to the Okaya Manufacturing Site in Japan, followed by some research afterward, gave me a lesson in a subject I’d never understood particularly well. I wanted to understand how the glass inside a lens is crafted, how the tools used in that process are prepared, and how people learn to do that work.

The facility was OM Digital Solutions’ Okaya Manufacturing Site in Nagano Prefecture, Japan. This was an overwhelming experience from a learning standpoint, so there was quite a bit that went over my head as we moved from station to station. Luckily, follow-up discussions with OM SYSTEM and research helped me fill in some of the gaps.

Okaya is the first optical lens manufacturing site in Japan for OM Digital Solutions, the company behind OM SYSTEM. It opened in 2025 and does two jobs. It produces lenses that are made in small quantities but come in many different types, and it works as a pilot factory, a place where the manufacturing processes for technically demanding new lenses are developed and proven before they’re used at scale.

The site works closely with the optical design team at the company’s headquarters in Hachioji, Tokyo. Designing a lens and figuring out how to build it are two different jobs that call for different expertise. Okaya’s engineers handle the second one, turning a design into a production process that actually works.

Mass production happens at the company’s factory in Vietnam. Before a production line for a new lens launches there, Okaya verifies the production technology, the manufacturing processes, and the work methods it will use. Working those out in Japan first is meant to make production in Vietnam more efficient and keep the quality consistent.

The place to begin is with an individual lens element, one of the many pieces of glass inside a camera lens. OM SYSTEM’s M.Zuiko Digital ED 40-150mm F2.8 PRO, for example, contains 16 of these elements. Before the lens can be assembled, each of these pieces of glass needs the correct curve and a smooth surface.

A piece of glass can be clear and look correct but still bend light the wrong way. A lens bends light to bring an image into focus on the camera’s sensor. Light from each point in the scene needs to come together at a matching point on the sensor. The curves of the glass help direct it there. If a curve is wrong, that light can spread around its intended point instead, making a small detail look blurry.

The sequence OM SYSTEM showed us at the Okaya Manufacturing Site starts with grinding, which gradually wears down the glass to form the basic curve. Finer grinding makes smaller adjustments to the glass. Polishing then wears away more material to give the surface the smoothness and accuracy it needs.

I got a small taste of this myself. During a workshop at Okaya, I tried lens polishing, including mounting the lens and taking it off again afterward. It looked simple. Then a slight mistake in my setup chipped the lens. That was enough to show me how delicate the process is and how much care and precision it takes.

Glass can look clear and smooth to the naked eye and still have flaws that affect the photograph. Tiny scratches, bumps, and dips, or a surface that strays slightly from its intended shape, can scatter light in directions it shouldn’t go. That can cause flare, the haze or bright spots stray light leaves in a picture, and lower the contrast, so the image looks flatter.

If the surface doesn’t match its designed shape, light won’t bend and come together the way the designers intended. So polishing has two jobs: leave the surface free of scratches, and reproduce the designed shape to within nanometers, or billionths of a meter. The engineers check the glass with a range of measuring instruments, but they also rely on experience and skill to make delicate adjustments to each lens.

Then they have to do it again on the next piece of glass, and the one after that. Even a slight difference between individual lenses can change how light travels through the finished lens and affect image quality.

Each glass element also needs to sit in the right position inside the lens. Imagine fitting one into a holder. It could fit neatly while the curved faces that bend light sit slightly off-center. That mismatch can send light to the wrong place. A manufacturing step called centering corrects that mismatch before assembly.

Getting the curve right and getting the glass into the right position both matter to the photograph. Even when we focus correctly, errors in the glass’s shape or alignment can leave fine details looking soft.

Even the tools OM Digital Solutions uses at the Okaya Manufacturing Site need preparation before they can work on the glass. These are the parts fitted to the machines that grind and polish the lens elements. The tools the engineers use to work on the glass need smooth, accurately made surfaces, too.

One of these tools has a small, round face that touches the glass. To prepare it, an engineer uses a second tool: a disc on the end of a handle. The engineer holds the disc against the first tool’s face, polishing the two surfaces together.

The accuracy of the tool affects the accuracy of the surface it produces on the glass.

I was surprised to see that they still prepare some of their tools by hand. The precision required helped me appreciate the care the engineers bring to preparing those tools and building the lenses. At Okaya, I saw veteran engineers working alongside younger colleagues to pass on their skills. Both generations were full of excitement and pride as they showed us how they make lenses in their facility.

That exchange between generations is a big part of how the skills developed at the Okaya Manufacturing Site get passed down. OM Digital Solutions says the younger engineers’ questions also encourage the veterans to keep improving their own skills. While watching them work, I could see how explaining a familiar task to someone else can make you think more carefully about the way you do it.

The training follows an apprenticeship model, with coaching taking place during manufacturing work such as polishing. Part of the challenge is passing on knowledge that comes from experience and can be difficult to put into written instructions.

With its younger engineers in mind, the company is also exploring other ways to pass on the skills and judgment that are hard to capture in a written document.

Along with their manufacturing skills, OM Digital Solutions also wants the experienced engineers to pass on their way of thinking about the work.

If I were explaining one of my photographs to another photographer, I’d want to talk about why I chose a particular aperture for depth of field or focused on a certain part of the scene. Understanding those choices could help them make decisions about their own photographs. Knowing why a manufacturing step is done a certain way could help younger engineers decide what to keep and where to make improvements. They can build on that experience to improve both how lenses are made and how those lenses perform.

When a photographer buys a lens, they expect it to meet the same standard as other copies of that model. That depends on being able to make its components accurately, again and again.

At Okaya, engineers test early versions of lens components for new products. They also check new manufacturing methods to see whether they are suitable for producing lenses in larger quantities. Once those methods have been checked, they can be transferred to the factory in Vietnam.

Some of this involves tasks as routine as loading parts into machines and taking them out again. They are automating repetitive jobs like these to help improve production quality and efficiency.

The relationship between the two sites continues long after production begins. If an issue turns up while a mass-production process is being verified at the Vietnam factory, the team at Okaya can reproduce the same issue on purpose. Recreating it gives the engineers a controlled way to analyze what went wrong, find the root cause, and develop a fix. Each round of that back-and-forth turns highly specialized know-how into a process the factory can repeat with the same quality, lens after lens.

Learning about OM Digital Solutions’ Okaya Manufacturing Site helped me understand the work, passion, and dedication that go into their lens making. I had never given the process much thought and, I admit, I assumed it was easier than it actually is. The hand preparation of the tools was a good example. Once I understood how a tool’s accuracy affects the glass it works on, I could see why that preparation needed so much care.

It also showed me how seriously the company takes quality. Nearly every step I learned about, from measuring a polished surface to deliberately recreating a problem from the Vietnam factory, exists to make sure a lens performs the way it was designed to, and that the next copy does too.

Understanding the work gave me more respect for the engineers who showed it to us and for the experience they are passing on to younger colleagues. As a travel photographer, I’ve often taken my gear for granted. I now have a better idea of what goes into making a lens and a much greater appreciation for the lenses that have helped me document the world over the last 15 years.

#9074. Leica Is Celebrating 60 Years of Noctilux With a 240-Page Book

Leica Is Celebrating 60 Years of Noctilux With a 240-Page Book

Leica is celebrating the 60th anniversary of the Noctilux lens family with the launch of a book that is centered on the optical achievement over the years. “From the first series-produced Leica lens with aspherical surfaces to the newest wide-angle variant, this book tells the story of how an audacious idea became a legend,” Leica says.

The original Noctilux was introduced at the now-defunct Photokina trade fair in 1966. Leica describes this lens as one that sought to capture light at night (hence the name), going past where other lenses had reached their limits. Leica says the new book, titled Noctilux, documents the evolution of this lens called “king of the night” and the six decades of research and development it underwent.

“For the most part, the book concentrates on the lenses themselves. Introduced in 1966, the Noctilux 50 f/1.2 was the first in the range: two aspherical element surfaces made in series production — a first among lens manufacturers worldwide. Each lens was painstakingly made by hand, and less than 2,000 units were produced,” Leica explains.

“The successor model, developed by Dr. Walter Mandler in Midland, Canada, was the only lens in the series to do without aspherical surfaces: seven classically polished elements and one special glass sufficed to achieve a speed of f/1. The Noctilux 50 f/0.95 ASPH. then dared to cross a magical line that had always seemed unreachable: it broke the f/1 speed barrier. The Noctilux 75 f/1.25 ASPH. brought the 75 mm focal length to the series for the first time – perfectly calibrated for portrait photography. The last chapter belongs to the Noctilux 35 f/1.2, the first Noctilux with a focal length of 35mm.”

The remaining chapters in the 240-page book cover the development of aspherical technology from its inception to production today as well as interviews with those in the Noctilux research laboratory. It also includes photo essays by Ana María Arévalo Gosen, Alisa Martynova, Jason Roman, François Rousseau, Paolo Roversi and Satoru Watanabe. The book also includes an overview of all M-mount lenses in Leica’s history.

“The book launch will take place on November 27th 2026 in Wetzlar during the Leitz Photographica Auction. To mark this occasion, Leica Camera AG will also be opening the exhibition ‘60 Years of Noctilux’ in the foyer on the eve of the auction: five past and current Noctilux lenses, as well as photo material, make the series’ history tangible beyond the book’s pages,” Leica concludes.

The book will be available starting November 27 at all Leica Stores (physical and online) as well as the LFI Online Store for $75.

#9072. What Critics Say About ‘Avedon,’ Streaming Now on Netflix

What Critics Say About ‘Avedon,’ Streaming Now on Netflix

Academy Award-winning filmmaker Ron Howard’s new documentary about Richard Avedon, succinctly titled just Avedon, has arrived on Netflix, and is being lauded by critics. Early indications suggest it’s a must-watch, especially for photography fans.

“‘Avedon’ tells us much about the man, as remembered by his intimates at the New Yorker (Tina Brown, Adam Gopnik, Mr. Lahr, Hilton Als), where, in 1992, he became its first staff photographer. His gallerist and dealer, Larry Gagosian, adds much about Avedon the businessman and says a ‘Dovima’ once sold for $2 million. And we hear from many of the models with whom he worked over the years, including Beverly Johnson, Twiggy, Penelope Tree, Lauren Hutton and Isabella Rossellini, who always has something insightful to add and does so here,” writes The Wall Street Journal‘s John Anderson.

“The most personal and moving recollections, though, come from Avedon’s son, John, and from the subject himself, who among other things remembers that throughout his childhood, all the formal Avedon family photos included a dog. ‘We never owned a dog,’ he says. And while he bemoans ‘the sadness of borrowed dogs,’ the conclusion is left to us viewers: That Avedon learned, early on, that the image was everything.”

While Anderson’s review is unscored, it’s undoubtedly positive.

Over at Variety, Owen Gleiberman describes Howard’s Avedon as a “thrilling documentary.”

‘Avedon,’ Ron Howard’s documentary about the legendary photographer, is a fantastic movie. It’s the best documentary Ron Howard has made (my favorite before this: ‘The Beatles: Eight Days a Week’), and it’s been edited in a way that’s so supple and artful that its technique should be studied in filmmaking classes. (The film’s editor is Andrew Morreale.) Woven through the movie are hundreds of photographs that were shot by Richard Avedon, and there’s no question that the images are stunning, but the way the movie layers them into your consciousness is nearly musical in its finesse. And that helps to tell the very large story ‘Avedon’ is telling: how Richard Avedon changed the metaphysics of photography, shifting the way we see the world.

Gleiberman adds that Howard’s new documentary does a superb job of showing how Avedon, on the one hand, was engrossed in the world of high fashion and on the other, fascinated by much more important, human struggles and activism. The critic likewise notes that Avedon’s photography remains truly timeless, captivating, and inspiring.

For those who want to learn all about the technical details of Avedon’s photography, they might find Howard’s film lacking. It’s not because Howard doesn’t care, though, it’s because Avedon didn’t.

“Talk to him about f-stops and he would glaze over,” Gleiberman writes. It is another review without a score, but the praise is immense.

Film critic Peyton Robinson of Roger Ebert gives Avedon four stars, noting that Avedon is perhaps the “greatest portrait photographer who ever lived.”

“Scaling ISO, aperture, and shutter speeds was not his prowess; his humanity was. Through bewitching charm and empathy, Avedon harvested an evocative truth from each portrait session,” Robinson writes.

“Long before Avedon picked up a camera, photography had to earn its respect. Once it did, the practice still had stipulations: rigidities and qualifiers that gatekept which images got the special title of “art.” Fashion images were captured to look like paintings. Avedon made unabashed, unashamed photographs. He made an image not about the clothes, the clout, or the resume, but the root of a person.”

“The film is sleek and energetic and looks fantastic, offering a bounty of images, including many of the most famous ones; it has something of the feel of a magazine layout without ever trying to look like a magazine,” writes Robert Llyod for Los Angeles Times.

Time‘s Stephanie Zacharek calls Avedon a “gracefully constructed documentary about a great American photographer.”

“Avedon is a road map through his career, a lifetime of looking at faces and striving to capture the life that animates them, before it vanishes forever,” Zacharek concludes.

Like her fellow critics, Zacharek touches on the more difficult subject matter in Avedon, including the photographer’s difficult upbringing, complicated family life, and lifelong passion for photography and the power it offered.

While there aren’t enough scored critic reviews for Avedon to earn a Tomatometer score at the time of writing, every review counted thus far is positive. It is well on its way to being a certified fresh documentary and so far, all critics agree, it’s extremely well-made, enduringly fascinating, and an honest and compelling look at Richard Avedon, among the greatest and most accomplished photographers in history.

#9070. 39 Award-Winning Photos From the 1839 Awards Photographers of the Year Contest

39 Award-Winning Photos From the 1839 Awards Photographers of the Year Contest

The 1839 Awards has announced the winners of its annual Photographer of the Year contest, celebrating exceptional, creative photography across multiple categories. Photographers from nearly 80 different countries entered the 2026 edition.

Giacomo Marchione was named the International Photographer of the Year 2026 for his series, The Invisible. Marchione’s five striking photos show underwater sea creatures, illuminated by light against a stark black background.

“At night, the sea doesn’t sleep,” Marchione says. “When the sun sets and the sea seems to fall silent, one of nature’s most extraordinary spectacles begins: the vertical migration of plankton. Millions of organisms rise from the depths to the surface in this upward migration.”

Marchione is a celebrated Italian underwater photographer as well as a practicing orthopedic surgeon. Marchione’s passion for underwater photography began in 1992 when he obtained his first scuba diving certification on vacation. He has photographed underwater all over the globe, including in the Maldives, Indonesia, Malaysia, and, of course, off the coast of Italy.

Marchione is not only the overall contest winner, but he also won the Underwater category.

On the Non-Professional side of the competition, photographer Dammy Twitch took top honors for his series, What If We Lived Among Gods. It’s a medium-format 120 film analog series exploring “myth, divinity, and everyday Nigerian life.”

Apampa Oluwadamilola, known professionally as Dammy Twitch, was born in 1995 and raised in Oyo State, Nigeria. Twitch relocated to Lagos and built his fine art photography, film, and music career. He was named to the Forbes 30 Under 30 list in 2022 and has received numerous accolades since, including the Rolling Stone Africa Mwamkom Vanguard Award for Visual Storytelling this year.

Twitch’s directorial debut, Call of My Life, has become one of the top five highest-grossing films ever in West Africa.

In total, there are many category winners across both Professional and Non-Professional sections. They can all be viewed on the 1839 Awards website. PetaPixel has selected a smattering of award-winning photos to share below, but everyone is highly encouraged to go view them all, organized by category, on the 1839 Awards website.

#9069. As Route 66 shifts into its centennial year, preservation efforts accelerate

Highway star: in New Mexico, Albuquerque’s Route 66 Visitor Center, which opened last April, is home to restored roadside signs from along the 2,500-mile route Courtesy of Friends of the Orphan Signs

US Route 66 officially started on 11 November 1926 with the launch of the nation’s first federal highway system. With the spread of affordable automobiles after the Second World War, it became a destination. A unique vernacular culture formed along its almost 2,500 miles running through eight states from Chicago, Illinois to Santa Monica, California, from neon signs enticing travellers to themed motels to roadside attractions with concrete and fibreglass sculptures.

Route 66 was decommissioned in 1985, with the new highways bypassing its Art Deco service stations and mid-century diners. Now, 100 years after its debut, there are efforts across the country to preserve what survives from what was once the “Main Street of America”.

“We want to let people outside of Route 66 know that it’s more than what you think it is,” says Rhys Martin, manager of the Preserve Route 66 Initiative at the National Trust for Historic Preservation. “Most people think of ’57 Chevys and cheeseburgers and Marilyn Monroe, and there’s a lot of that, but there’s so much more. It ties together so many diverse cultures, from Native American to African American. In my home state of Oklahoma, it goes through the Asian District [in Oklahoma City], which sprung up around Vietnamese refugees during the war. In West Hollywood, Route 66 has a huge LGBTQ presence.”

Grants from the Preserve Route 66 Initiative reflect that range of history, which is often overlooked in the nostalgia for its Americana. There are structural repair needs, like at the Fanning 66 Outpost in Cuba, Missouri, which hosts a 42ft-high rocking chair (the world’s largest until 2015), as well as storytelling projects, such as mapping Native American experiences along the corridor, as it passes through many tribal and ancestral lands yet has had little representation of their voices. Care for the road extends to the scarce sections of its original pavement. Through local advocacy, what is known as the Ribbon Road in Ottawa County, Oklahoma, which has the last segment of a 9ft-wide design made for Model Ts, was partially protected from resurfacing this year.

“You might think a pavement’s not art, but when you get out and look at it, especially compared to what it is today, it is very different,” Martin says. “I have come to really appreciate it from a craftsmanship perspective, but also a longevity perspective. These are the same roads that the Model Ts went west on during the Dust Bowl to seek a better life, and the fact that I get to drive these same roads tells a story.”

Advocacy is under way to give National Historic Trail designation to Route 66, with a bipartisan bill introduced last year. Martin notes that Route 66 is now similar to how it was before 1926, when it was a loose network of roads, and this legislation would help bring together its fragmented parts.

“It gets people to sit at the same table, like the state Route 66 associations, the National Park Service and the Department of Transportation, so that we can find ways to work together for corridor-wide initiatives and to help elevate preservation needs,” he says. “The corridor continues to evolve, and buildings are threatened all the time with demolition or augmentation beyond recognition, and being designated as a National Historic Trail is not a roadblock. But it is something to say, this is important and we need to take care when the fabric of the road might be forever altered.”

Coca Cola painting on a brick wall, along Route 66 in Stroud, Oklahoma Courtesy National Trust for Historic Preservation

Local groups, municipalities and individuals are stewarding Route 66’s relics. Martin is also the president of the Oklahoma Route 66 Association, which is restoring a U-Haul painted by the late artist Bob Waldmire, who illustrated maps and postcards of the road’s built and natural wonders. The city of Catoosa in Oklahoma acquired the beloved roadside Blue Whale in 2020 from the family of Hugh S. Davis, who in 1972 sculpted the 80ft-long attraction from concrete as a gift for his wife. Last May, a new Blue Whale Visitor Center opened with retro illuminated signage.

The city of Albuquerque opened a Route 66 Visitor Center last April and its park features a collection of restored roadside signs. Among them is the first major project from the Friends of the Orphan Signs (FOS), an organisation that since 2010 has worked on revitalising abandoned signs, particularly in Albuquerque’s underserved neighbourhoods.

Lindsey Fromm, the executive director of FOS, says that many of these signs are for places that were razed during the city’s removal of derelict buildings: “There were areas of Route 66 with dozens of towering empty signs.”

Most Route 66 sign restorations return them to their former glory; FOS reimagines them as public art. Revivir (2012) at the new visitor centre was created with students who designed visuals responding to local nature that were bordered with purple neon.

“While artists lead these sign projects, they will collaborate with communities, archives, the surrounding environment, or will collect histories and stories to create the work that is displayed, so that it speaks to the immediate moment and surrounding community who live, work and travel by the sign,” Fromm says.

Projects like this are not just about preserving places for tourists but Route 66’s role in daily life. These grassroots and national efforts recognise that even though it is no longer a main thoroughfare, it is still a vital place of connection from the Midwest to the Pacific, for communities both urban and rural, and between the visitors and residents brought together on their journeys.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation is helping 30 congregations shore up their buildings and share their stories, with their communities and the world

The Hendrick I. Lott House in southeast Brooklyn—former home to a family of enslavers who later made it a stop on the Underground Railroad—will undergo a major preservation and renovation project next year

Selma’s long-abandoned Edistone Hotel, witness to 170 years of African American history, was recently saved by a non-profit devoted to protecting Black historical sites

The two-year grant Conserving Black Modernism extends the foundation's larger initiative to protect Modernist architecture

#9067. New Sensor Tech Could Replace Bayer Color Filter and Transform Mobile Photography

New Sensor Tech Could Replace Bayer Color Filter and Transform Mobile Photography

Metalenz has acquired Israeli startup PxE Imaging. PxE’s claim to fame is its Holocoder technology, a replacement for the Bayer color filter found on traditional image sensors.

As Metalenz explains in its press release, the Holocoder “eliminates the need for the Bayer filter and sorts light without absorption, increasing the light delivered to a standard image sensor by 2.5x.”

As expected, significantly increasing the light delivered to an image sensor will, all else equal, dramatically improve camera performance and image quality across the board—in dark scenes and bright ones alike.

Like PxE Imaging, Metalenz has been focused on technologies that adhere directly to an image sensor. A few years ago, Metalenz brought its groundbreaking metasurface optics to market, which are ultra-thin optics that can be printed like semiconductor wafers. The key is how the thin lens bends light.

That’s true, too, of Holocoder technology. The Holocoder “harnesses the wave nature of light to physically decode information such as wavelength and depth, enabling simultaneous capture of color and depth information in the same image with a single camera.”

A Bayer filter, which is how traditional digital image sensors capture and reconstruct color, also absorbs about 60% of the light coming into a sensor, Metalenz says. With its acquisition of PxE, Metalenz can now add sophisticated color and depth information to the material and surface data its products already capture, all without significantly increasing manufacturing complexity or computational demands.

“Metalenz has strategically expanded its IP from unique hardware to full-stack solutions co-designed with our metasurfaces,” says Rob Devlin, Co-founder and CEO of Metalenz.

“We’ve deployed into the most demanding customer devices, built a supply chain at mass-market scale, and built a software stack that takes information delivered to a sensor all the way through AI decisions. With PxE’s technology and team, we’re expanding our capabilities into visible sensing, addressing a longstanding problem of low light performance while solving the new physical AI problem of obtaining richer information beyond conventional RGB imagery,” Devlin continues.

“Owning hardware that brings new information to sensors is the real moat for differentiated AI models. Our combined capability with PxE extends that same principle across all of machine vision, so people and machines can see and understand more about the world without relying on heavy computation.”

“We developed the Holocoder to capture information in light that conventional sensors discard or cannot see, giving cameras greater light sensitivity and the ability to capture color and depth together,” adds Yoav Berlatzky, Co-founder and CEO of PxE Imaging.

“Joining Metalenz gives us the manufacturing platform and commercial reach to bring this technology to everyday devices. Together, we can give people better images and machines a richer understanding of the world.”

The terms of the transaction have not been disclosed.

Devlin spoke to WIRED about the acquisition, shedding more light, pun intended, on PxE Imaging’s technology.

“Apple, Samsung, Google — everyone is fighting to improve the visible camera every year, right?” Devlin tells WIRED.

“A lot of what they’re doing is investing hundreds of millions of dollars into software to try to somehow improve it, but the downside of that is that once information is lost when you’re absorbing all of that light, you can’t really buy it back, even if you’re throwing all of the software into the world at it.”

As of right now, Metalenz cannot directly combine PxE’s Holocoder technology with its commercial Metalenz optics. However, it is absolutely in the cards for the long term. PxE’s technology itself could hit the market as soon as the end of next year, thanks to Metalenz’s manufacturing capacity.

The potential use cases here are manifold. In scenarios where tiny cameras are very important, like autonomous vehicles for example, it’s obvious that a smaller camera that can absorb more light is beneficial.

Another obvious situation is smartphone cameras. As Devlin notes, there is a physical problem that image sensors of all sizes must try to overcome: getting more, better light data. The more light that reaches the sensor, the better. The Bayer color filter is an incredible technological achievement, but it’s getting very long in the tooth. Perhaps, if PxE is correct, there’s a better way.

Image creditsMetalenz, PxE Imaging. Header photo licensed via Depositphotos.com.

Airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently shows:

The savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (New York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

One important note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

The old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

What does matter is how far in advance you book. Here are the optimal booking windows based on aggregate data from Hopper, Google Flights, and CheapAir analyses of millions of fares:

The general pattern is that prices start high when flights first open (9-11 months out), drop to their lowest point in the 1-3 month window as airlines compete for bookings, then spike in the final 2-3 weeks as remaining seats become scarce. Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

The right tools eliminate the need to manually check prices. Here is what works best and how to use each one:

Fare alerts are the single most effective strategy for the time-constrained FI-minded traveler. Set alerts on Google Flights for every trip you are considering in the next 6 months. You will receive email notifications when prices drop, and you can book immediately without daily searching. This passive approach consistently saves $50 to $300 per ticket.

For those building a travel rewards strategy, credit card travel portals (Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Travel, Capital One Travel) sometimes offer slightly better prices than booking direct. More importantly, points earned through everyday spending can cover flights entirely. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into 50,000 points — enough for 1-2 round-trip domestic flights. The FI approach to travel rewards is not to spend more to earn points, but to redirect spending you would do anyway through a rewards-earning card and let the points accumulate passively.

The single biggest predictor of cheap airfare is not when you book or which tool you use — it is how flexible you are with dates and destinations. Google Flights date grid and Skyscanner everywhere search exist specifically to help flexible travelers find the cheapest options. Being willing to fly on a Tuesday instead of a Friday, or to visit Portugal instead of France, routinely saves 30-50% compared to fixed-date, fixed-destination searches. For FI-minded travelers, flexibility is a skill that pays dividends on every trip.

Tuesday and Wednesday are consistently the cheapest days to fly domestically, with fares typically 15-25% below Friday and Sunday prices. Saturday can also be a good value for departures. The savings are largest on popular leisure routes where weekend demand creates the biggest price swings.

No. The idea that booking on Tuesday at midnight gets you the best price is a myth. Airlines adjust prices thousands of times per day using dynamic pricing algorithms. What matters is booking within the optimal window (1-3 months out for domestic flights) and setting fare alerts to catch price drops.

For domestic flights, 1 to 3 months before departure is the sweet spot. For international flights, 2 to 8 months is optimal. Holiday travel should be booked 2 to 4 months ahead. Booking too early (6+ months for domestic) or too late (under 2 weeks) typically results in higher prices.

Sometimes. Spirit, Frontier, and other ultra-low-cost carriers advertise base fares 40-60% below major airlines but charge separately for carry-on bags ($35-$65), seat selection ($5-$50), and other extras. For a traveler with no checked bag and no seat preference, budget carriers save real money. For families or anyone checking bags, compare total cost including all fees — major airlines are often competitive.

Yes. The cheapest times to fly domestically are January (after the 7th), February (excluding Valentine week), early March, late April, September, October, and early November. The most expensive periods are the weeks around Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and the peak summer window from mid-June through mid-August.

Travel rewards cards earn points on everyday spending that can be redeemed for flights. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into enough points for 1-2 domestic round trips. The FI-aligned approach is to use a rewards card for purchases you would make anyway (groceries, gas, utilities) and let points accumulate passively — never spend more just to earn points.

Finding cheap flights comes down to three principles: be flexible with dates (fly Tuesday or Wednesday for 15-25% savings), book in the right window (1-3 months for domestic, 2-8 for international), and let technology do the searching (Google Flights fare alerts catch drops automatically). Combined with a travel rewards card that earns points on everyday spending, these strategies make air travel significantly more affordable without requiring hours of research. Set your alerts, stay flexible, and book when the price is right.

#9062. This Retro-Inspired Waist-Level Digital Camera Already Raised $270K on Kickstarter

This Retro-Inspired Waist-Level Digital Camera Already Raised $270K on Kickstarter

A new retro-inspired digital camera with a waist-level viewfinder has quickly raised nearly $270,000 on Kickstarter, absolutely shattering its meager $4,996 funding target.

The Campix, as Kosmo Foto writes, is made by Hong Kong-based photo brand Fotorgear. As Kosmo Foto notes, the Campix is “heavily influenced by the East German Exakta Varex camera,” including its waist-level prism. For its part, Fotorgear says the Campix is “inspired by the timeless design of classic waist-level film cameras.”

The company adds that its new camera combines a retro waist-level viewfinder and an analog-like experience with the convenience of digital. To that end, the Campix embraces tactile manual controls, film-inspired digital simulations, and a virtual “film” roll experience.

The Campix is far from the first camera to offer a “roll” style shooting experience, with perhaps the most famous example being the Fujifilm X half. The idea is that users select their preferred “film” look and then shoot through an entire 36-shot “roll” of digital images using that style. Photographers can also customize these looks in an accompanying app and save them to one of six filter slots, which can be cycled through on the camera using a physical dial.

Notably, the Campix does two things very differently from other film-inspired digital cameras—beyond its signature waist-level viewfinder. First, the camera features interchangeable lenses thanks to its proprietary T-mount design. Second, the Campix captures RAW files, a feature missing from many style-focused, film-emulation digital cameras.

As for its optics, users can swap between an 8mm fisheye, 16mm wide-angle, 60mm portrait, 75mm macro, and a 1.55x anamorphic lens. Fotorgear also sells these same lenses for use with smartphones. The stock lens is a 26mm-equivalent f/2.2 prime.

The Campix includes a Xenon flash with TTL support; Fotorgear states the flash has an effective range of about one to three meters.

Internally, the camera is built around a 13-megapixel Sony IMX258 image sensor. This Type 1/3.06 sensor is similar in size to the ultra-wide and telephoto sensors found in many smartphones, carrying a crop factor of roughly 7.4x. The camera offers Auto ISO (100–3,200) alongside automatic exposure, while white balance can be set to automatic or manual.

As mentioned, the Campix pairs with a mobile companion app available for iOS and Android, as well as a dedicated desktop app for RAW processing.

The Campix Basic starts at $109 for early-bird backers and will retail for $209, bundled with the 26mm lens. The Campix Set—priced at $199 for super-early birds and $319 at retail—includes the camera body, the standard 26mm lens, plus the 75mm Macro, 60mm Portrait, and 16mm Wide-Angle lenses. It also comes with a Star Filter, CPL, and UV filter set. The lenses can also be purchased individually.

#9060. Photogenic ‘One-in-a-Million’ Fish With Xanthochromism Caught in New York

Photogenic ‘One-in-a-Million’ Fish With Xanthochromism Caught in New York

U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) biologists caught a one-in-a-million fish in Oswego, New York, and it sure is a looker.

Biologists performing a routine Aquatic Invasive Species Survey in Oswego Harbor, New York, caught a burbot (Lota lota) with xanthochromism, a “rare biological condition” that turns the fish bright yellow-orange. Burbot are typically brown with dark spots, making this almost entirely yellow-orange specimen a remarkable find.

Xanthochromism is a rare genetic mutation that suppresses normal dark pigmentation, producing a distinct yellow-orange appearance. Scientists note that xanthochromism is “considerably less common” in wild fish populations than albinism or melanism.

In 2024, an orange shark made headlines and scientists later determined that it had an even rarer combination of albinism and xanthochromism. Its unusual eyes the result of the former and the neon-orange skin the latter.

Because burbot are a native species, they are not the primary target of the Aquatic Invasive Species Early Detection and Monitoring Program. As the USFWS explains, this program deploys advanced technology and targeted surveillance strategies to locate “watchlist species” across New York’s Great Lakes, rivers, and harbors.

Most fish caught during these surveys are native species, which biologists inspect and safely release. Burbot—even typical specimens—are notable catches due to their low populations in the Great Lakes. Finding a burbot with xanthochromism is exceptionally rare.

According to United States Geological Survey (USGS) biologists on the team, this particular individual appeared emaciated and in poor health. Consequently, scientists transported it to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for detailed analysis.

“The discovery could turn out to be lucky for the species too; this exceptionally rare fish may provide valuable insight into the health of the species’ populations throughout the basin that can inform management actions,” USFWS says.

While scientists documented this recent discovery, wildlife photographers have also captured extraordinarily rare animals over the years. In 2024, wildlife photographer Yves Adams photographed an ultra-rare all-black penguin.

It was not Adams’ first time photographing extremely rare birds. A few years prior, he photographed what he believes was a “never-before-seen” yellow penguin — not unlike the burbot recently found in New York.

#9058. Could Firenze Lai’s first UK solo show signal a shift in global market recognition for Hong Kong artists?

Firenze Lai, who has lived in London since 2022 © White Cube/Ollie Hammick

In mid-October, coinciding with Frieze London and nearly four years after she relocated from her native Hong Kong to London, the artist Firenze Lai opened her first UK solo exhibition at White Cube Mason’s Yard. Featuring new works created in her adopted home, North and True North (until 14 November) is not just a milestone for her career, it also signals a potential shift in major galleries’ approach to Asia.

Lai is among a handful of Hong Kong artists represented by major Western blue-chip galleries today. Born in 1984 and educated in Hong Kong, the artist has exhibited internationally, including in the main exhibition of the 57th Venice Biennale in 2017. Her current show marks the first solo exhibition White Cube has staged by an artist originating from Hong Kong since it opened its outpost in the city in 2012.

The shift suggests the maturity of this generation of mid-career artists from Hong Kong, several of whom have relocated abroad fairly recently. It also raises hopes that Western blue-chip galleries are finally adopting a less siloed approach to Asia, in which global art markets were approached from a simplistic geographical perspective. This mindset of “keeping Asians in Asia” kept transnational relationships rare, the cultural strategist Adeline Ooi notes, but this is starting to change.

“People are much more cosmopolitan and international today. They are not just rooted within their region and bounded by their geographies,” says Ooi, the former director for Asia at Art Basel.

Major international galleries are taking a more sophisticated approach, rather than simply placing Asian artists in front of Asian collectors, says the Taipei- and New York-based art adviser Gladys Lin. “It’s about integrating that artist into the wider language of the gallery programme, so that collectors from different backgrounds can understand the work in relation to other artists, histories and conversations.”

Hong Kong has long been Asia’s biggest art market hub, with headline-grabbing auction sales for over half a century joined, since the 2000s, by a lively landscape of galleries and fairs catering to local collectors, and those from mainland China and the wider region. The city has hosted Art Basel Hong Kong since 2013, and Asian outposts of blue-chip galleries proliferated after the launch of the ArtHK fair in 2008. Artists from the city, however, have struggled to receive much attention in the global market, or even at home.

Leading multinational Western blue-chip galleries such as White Cube, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, Gagosian and Pace have shown Asian artists internationally, but they tend to concentrate on bolstering their rosters with established names from Asian cultural powerhouses like mainland China, South Korea and Japan.

Firenze Lai’s A Second Storm (2025) from her White Cube show Photo: © White Cube/Theo Christelis; © the artist

Hongkonger artists are increasingly exhibiting abroad, but primarily with smaller galleries. The Taipei-based artist Lee Kit works with galleries including Massimo de Carlo in London and ShugoArts in Tokyo. The UK-based Chris Huen Sin-kan showed with the now-defunct Simon Lee in New York and London, and more recently with Matt Carey-Williams.

While diaspora and émigré Hongkongers have more opportunities to cultivate overseas networks, artists based in the city are also widening their reach. Chang Ya Chin held her first solo show with Perrotin in New York in 2025, while Stephen Wong Chun-hei exhibited with Unit London in 2022 and Mother’s Tankstation in 2025, which also represents Lee Kit. The sound artist Samson Young performed his work Canon at Art Basel Unlimited in 2016, presented by Cologne’s Galerie Gisela Capitain and the now-closed Team Gallery. Wong Ping held a solo show at Tanya Bonakdar Gallery in New York in 2021, while Mak2 had her European gallery solo debut in 2023 with the now-defunct Peres Projects in Berlin.

However, representation by one of the global “big five” galleries remains rare for Hong Kong artists. White Cube began working with Lai in July 2025. “Her paintings have a singularity that speaks to the human condition, a universal theme that audiences everywhere can appreciate,” a spokesperson for the gallery says.

Lai was born and raised in Hong Kong, and has lived in London since 2022. Her visual language nonetheless remains rooted in her lived experience of her densely populated hometown. “We are not 100% Chinese, nor are we 100% British,” Lai says.

Moving to London changed how she approaches the canvas. The painter recalls that during her time in Hong Kong—where she built a solid career and a following for her dreamlike figurative paintings through a long-term and continuing collaboration with Guangzhou gallery Vitamin Creative Space—she tended to work on smaller canvases.

“After moving to London, I felt that I needed a bigger canvas. I have a lot more to say,” Lai says. Much of her poignant new work draws from deep emotional responses to her changing environment before and after relocating.

Lai says the current timing for global market recognition for Hong Kong artists makes sense. Those of her generation, born between the late 1970s and 90s, needed time to establish themselves and explore which galleries would be a good fit for their career. “I am proud of the fact that Hong Kong has produced a generation of artists who can have solo shows in London,” she says. “I’ve been told to give up many times. But I can now tell a 15-year-old [aspiring artist] that this is possible.”

It remains unclear how much long-term benefit a solo exhibition at a global gallery can bring to an artist’s career. “Who are the people paying attention to Firenze right now? If they are private collectors, who are they and what are their demographics? If it’s an institution, who are they?” Ooi asks. Expanding the following for her work will take time as much as exposure.

Lin says Lai’s move to London put her into a different art world, where she offers galleries a “compelling combination”. “She already comes with a collector base in Asia, an institutional history and more than a decade of critical exposure,” Lin says. “It’s not simply about bringing in Asian collectors, but about adding an artist who connects different collectors, institutional and geographical systems. For a global gallery today, geography can still be a useful entry point, but it cannot be the final framework.”
